specPoints.text: understand how the similarities in the reactions of these elements with water provide evidence for their recognition as a family of elements
understand how the differences between the reactions of these elements with air and water provide evidence for the trend in reactivity in Group1
use knowledge of trends in Group1 to predict the properties of other alkali metals

primer.text: You already know from Atomic Structure that electrons sit in shells around the nucleus, and that an atom's chemistry depends heavily on its outermost shell. That single idea carries this whole note: the alkali metals each hold one outer electron, and everything from their softness to their ferocious water reactions flows from it.

lessons.title: Group 1 elements
sourceHeadings: How Alkali Metals React with Water
lessons.opening: The first column of the periodic table holds a family so consistent in its behaviour that it carries its own name: the alkali metals. Drop any of them into water and you get the same story, an alkaline solution plus bubbles of hydrogen. That shared pattern of reactions is the evidence chemists use to recognise them as one family.
keyPoints: The alkali metals are lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium, caesium and francium, found in the first column.
They share characteristic chemical behaviour because each carries a single electron in its outermost shell.
They are soft, easily cut with a knife, with low densities and low melting points.
All react with water to give an alkaline solution, which is how the family earned its name.
The family equation: a Group 1 metal plus water yields a metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas.

low.restatement: Every member of the first column reacts with water in the same way, giving a metal hydroxide and hydrogen; that shared pattern is the family's calling card.
low.analogy: It is like recognising siblings at a family party: different heights, but the same laugh, and the laugh here is the reaction with water.
low.examPointer: Equations must carry state symbols: 2Na (s) + 2H2O (l) gives 2NaOH (aq) + H2 (g); the exam hint in the note stresses exactly this.

medium.restatement: One outer electron per atom explains both the shared chemistry and the family's softness, low density and low melting points; losing that lone electron is easy, so reactivity runs high.
medium.analogy: Think of a row of vending machines that all accept the same coin: present water, and every one of them dispenses the same product, an alkaline solution.
medium.examPointer: When asked for evidence of family membership, quote the matching reaction pattern with water rather than mere position in the same column.

check.stem: Why are the Group 1 metals called the alkali metals?

options.text: They form alkaline solutions when they react with water
options.explanation: The name records the family's signature reaction with water.

options.text: Because they sit in the first column of the periodic table
options.explanation: Position earned them the Group 1 label; the alkali name comes from their water chemistry.

options.text: Because they are soft enough to cut with a knife
options.explanation: Softness is a family property but not the source of the name.
options.misconception: physical property mistaken for naming reason

check.stem: Which feature explains why the alkali metals share so many chemical properties?

options.text: Each has a single electron in its outermost shell
options.explanation: One outer electron is the shared structure behind the family's common chemistry.

options.text: Each has a full outermost shell
options.explanation: A full outer shell describes the noble gases; the alkali metals hold one electron beyond a full shell.

options.text: Each has the same number of neutrons
options.explanation: Neutron counts differ across the family; chemistry follows electrons.

check.stem: Which equation, complete with state symbols, correctly shows sodium reacting with water?

options.text: 2Na (s) + 2H2O (l) gives 2NaOH (aq) + H2 (g)
options.explanation: Both the balancing and the state symbols match the family pattern.

options.text: Na (s) + H2O (l) gives NaOH (aq) + H2 (g)
options.explanation: The hydrogen atoms do not balance; two water molecules are required.

options.text: 2Na (s) + 2H2O (l) gives NaOH2 (aq) + H2 (g)
options.explanation: The hydroxide formula is NaOH; a sodium ion pairs with one hydroxide ion.

options.text: Na (s) + H2O (l) gives NaO (aq) + H2 (g)
options.explanation: With water the product is the hydroxide; oxides form with oxygen, as in the air reaction.

check.stem: Which set of physical properties belongs to the alkali metals?

options.text: Soft, low density, low melting points
options.explanation: These are the family's listed physical traits.

options.text: Hard, high density, very high melting points
options.explanation: That profile fits transition metals such as iron, not Group 1.

options.text: Dull, brittle, gaseous at room temperature
options.explanation: Those traits describe non-metals; alkali metals are bright solids when freshly cut.

check.stem: What is the evidence that the alkali metals belong to one chemical family?

options.text: Their reactions with water follow the same pattern and give the same kinds of products
options.explanation: Matching reaction patterns are the chemical evidence for family membership.

options.text: They all sit in the same column of the periodic table
options.explanation: Position groups them, but the chemical evidence is the shared reaction pattern.

options.text: They all look identical when freshly cut
options.explanation: Appearance is superficial; family membership rests on shared chemical behaviour.

check.stem: State the family name of the metals found in the first column of the periodic table.
check.modelAnswer: The alkali metals — lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium, caesium and francium.

check.stem: State the two products formed when any Group 1 metal reacts with water.
check.modelAnswer: A metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas.

check.stem: Explain why all the alkali metals share the same characteristic chemical behaviour.
check.modelAnswer: Because each of them carries a single electron in its outermost shell, so they react in the same characteristic ways.

check.stem: A student finds a metal that can be cut easily with a knife. State the family it likely belongs to, and one other physical property it should show.
check.modelAnswer: An alkali metal — they are soft and easily cut, with low densities and low melting points.

lessons.title: Trends in Group 1
lessons.opening: Descend the group and the water reactions escalate: lithium fizzes steadily, sodium dashes across the surface, potassium ignites with a lilac flame. In air the pattern repeats, with tarnishing growing faster the further down you go. Even the physical properties slide in step, as softness increases and melting points fall.
keyPoints: Reactions with water grow more vigorous on descending the group, from fizzing lithium to flaming potassium.
Lithium fizzes gently on the water surface, sodium races about, and potassium burns with a lilac flame.
Exposed to air, each metal tarnishes as oxygen draws a dull oxide coating across its surface.
Tarnishing also speeds up down the group, mirroring the water trend.
Melting points fall down the group as the attractive forces between outer electrons and positive ions weaken.

low.restatement: Down the group: faster fizzing, livelier movement, a lilac flame for potassium, quicker tarnishing in air, softer metal, lower melting point.
low.analogy: It reads like a risk dial being turned up floor by floor: each level down, the same reactions simply get louder.
low.examPointer: Observation questions want specifics: name the lilac flame for potassium or the drifting movement for lithium, not just the word vigorous.

medium.restatement: The water and oxygen trends run parallel because both reflect the same easing of electron loss, while melting points fall as the attractive forces weaken down the group.
medium.analogy: Picture a set of speakers turned up as you walk downstairs; each alkali metal plays the same tune, only louder, and the oxide coat appears sooner.
medium.examPointer: Trends are patterns, not rules, so an odd result does not break the group; state the pattern and treat exceptions as quirks, exactly as the note's hint says.

check.stem: How do the water reactions of the alkali metals change on descending the group?

options.text: They become more vigorous
options.explanation: Lithium's gentle fizzing is the mild end; the violence grows downward.

options.text: They become gentler
options.explanation: The trend runs the other way; potassium, not lithium, ignites.

options.text: They stay identical throughout
options.explanation: The products stay the same, but the intensity climbs steadily.
options.misconception: family similarity mistaken for uniform intensity

check.stem: Potassium is dropped onto water. Which observation set fits?

options.text: It burns with a lilac flame and skims very rapidly across the surface
options.explanation: Both observations are the ones listed for potassium.

options.text: It fizzes gently and drifts slowly on the surface
options.explanation: That gentle set describes lithium, the quietest of the three.

options.text: It dissolves without any fizzing at all
options.explanation: Hydrogen bubbles are released in every alkali-metal water reaction.

check.stem: Why do alkali metals tarnish in air, and how does the tarnishing change down the group?

options.text: Oxygen forms a dull oxide coating, and tarnishing speeds up down the group
options.explanation: Both halves match the note: oxide coating first, faster tarnishing downward.

options.text: Water vapour rusts the surface, and tarnishing slows down the group
options.explanation: Rust is iron-specific; the coating is an oxide, and it forms faster down the group.

options.text: The shiny surface fades through friction alone
options.explanation: Tarnish is a chemical reaction with oxygen, not simple wear.
options.misconception: physical wear mistaken for chemical change

check.stem: What happens to melting points down Group 1, and why?

options.text: They decrease, because the attractive forces between outer electrons and positive ions weaken
options.explanation: The stated cause and the stated direction both match the note.

options.text: They increase, because the atoms grow heavier
options.explanation: Heavier atoms do not bond more strongly here; the metallic bonding weakens downward.

options.text: They stay constant, because trends apply only to reactivity
options.explanation: Physical properties trend too; the note's own graph shows the melting-point fall.

check.stem: Which statement about density is supported by the note?

options.text: The first three alkali metals are less dense than water
options.explanation: That is the stated density fact for lithium, sodium and potassium.

options.text: Every alkali metal floats on water
options.explanation: Only the first three are stated to float; rubidium is already denser than potassium.

options.text: Density falls steadily down the group
options.explanation: The prediction for rubidium runs the other way: denser than potassium.

check.stem: State how lithium's and sodium's reactions with water differ.
check.modelAnswer: Lithium fizzes gently on the water surface, while sodium races about — the reaction grows more vigorous down the group.

check.stem: State what forms on the surface of an alkali metal left exposed to air.
check.modelAnswer: A dull oxide coating — oxygen draws the coating across the shiny surface.

check.stem: Explain why melting points fall on descending Group 1.
check.modelAnswer: Because the attractive forces between the outer electrons and the positive ions weaken down the group, so less energy is needed to melt the metal.

check.stem: Francium sits at the bottom of Group 1. State whether francium should tarnish in air faster or slower than potassium does.
check.modelAnswer: Faster — tarnishing speeds up down the group, mirroring the water-reaction trend.

lessons.title: Predicting properties in Group 1
lessons.opening: Trends are only useful if they let you reach beyond the metals you have met. Position rubidium or caesium below potassium in the group and the patterns point forward for you: expect greater vigour in water and air, plus lower melting points and higher densities. Lithium, at the top, anchors the gentle end of the family.
keyPoints: Rubidium, caesium and francium should out-react the first three metals with both air and water.
Lithium heads the family as least reactive; francium, at the bottom, would be most reactive.
Rubidium is predicted to be a soft grey solid, shiny when freshly cut.
Its density should exceed potassium's and its melting point should sit lower still.

low.restatement: Below potassium, predict more violence with water and air, a softer metal, a lower melting point and a higher density.
low.analogy: Forecasting an alkali metal is like forecasting weather further along the same front: same pattern, turned up a notch.
low.examPointer: Describing an unseen metal's reaction invites strong words such as violently or explosively, so choose them deliberately.

medium.restatement: Rubidium is the worked prediction: soft grey solid, shiny when freshly cut, denser than potassium, melting below it; caesium and francium extend the same logic further.
medium.analogy: It is like walking into a cinema series one episode late: the story continues in the direction already established, only more so.
medium.examPointer: Anchor each prediction to a named trend, then quote the reference values, such as potassium's 0.86 g cm-3 density or its 63.5 degrees Celsius melting point.

check.stem: Caesium sits below potassium in Group 1. How should its reaction with water compare?

options.text: More violent still, with words like explosively appropriate
options.explanation: Descending the group means stronger reactions, and the note's own hint backs such wording.

options.text: Gentler, because the reactivity is spent by then
options.explanation: Nothing is spent; the vigour keeps rising down the group.

options.text: Identical to potassium in every way
options.explanation: The product pattern repeats, but the intensity does not.
options.misconception: family uniformity mistaken for identical intensity

check.stem: Which alkali metal is the least reactive?

options.text: Lithium, at the top of the group
options.explanation: Reactivity rises downward, so the top member is the least reactive.

options.text: Francium, at the bottom
options.explanation: Francium would be the most reactive; the quiet end is the top.

options.text: Sodium, because it is the most familiar
options.explanation: Familiarity says nothing; sodium sits mid-group and is outpaced below.

check.stem: Predict rubidium's melting point relative to potassium's 63.5 degrees Celsius.

options.text: Lower, because melting points fall down the group
options.explanation: The falling melting-point trend carries directly to rubidium.

options.text: Higher, because heavier metals melt at hotter temperatures
options.explanation: That intuition fits transition metals; Group 1 melts cooler on the way down.

options.text: Unpredictable without measuring it
options.explanation: The whole point of the trends is to make exactly this prediction.

check.stem: Which prediction set correctly describes freshly cut rubidium?

options.text: A soft grey solid that looks shiny when freshly cut
options.explanation: Both traits come straight from the note's rubidium predictions.

options.text: A hard dull metal that cannot be cut
options.explanation: Both halves contradict the family: alkali metals are soft and bright when cut.

options.text: A flaky pale solid with a very high melting point
options.explanation: Flakiness and high melting points belong elsewhere; rubidium stays soft and low-melting.

check.stem: Why is it sound to predict francium's behaviour from the group trends, even though it is barely ever seen?

options.text: Trends are patterns that extend down the group, so francium should out-react caesium, though odd results remain possible
options.explanation: This is exactly the trend-based prediction the note models, with the trends-not-rules caveat respected.

options.text: Trends are strict rules, so francium must behave exactly as predicted
options.explanation: The note's hint says trends are not rules; exceptions can appear without breaking the pattern.

options.text: Francium cannot be predicted at all from Group 1 chemistry
options.explanation: The family pattern is exactly what licenses predictions about unseen members.

check.stem: State which Group 1 metal is the most reactive, and where it sits in the group.
check.modelAnswer: Francium, at the bottom of the group (lithium, at the top, is the least reactive).

check.stem: State which Group 1 metals should out-react lithium, sodium and potassium with both air and water.
Explain why francium is predicted to be the most reactive alkali metal.
check.modelAnswer: Because the metals grow more reactive with both air and water on descending the group, and francium sits at the very bottom.

check.stem: Caesium sits below rubidium in Group 1. Predict whether caesium's melting point is lower or higher than rubidium's.
check.modelAnswer: Lower — melting points fall on descending the group, and caesium sits below rubidium.

glossary.definition: The Group 1 metals, lithium to francium, which form alkaline solutions when they react with water.
A solution with a pH above 7; the product formed when an alkali metal meets water.
The soluble, colourless product of an alkali metal's reaction with water, of general formula MOH.
Letters in brackets after each formula in an equation, recording solid, liquid, gas or aqueous state.
The dull oxide coating that forms on a metal surface when oxygen attacks it.
A pattern of behaviour that changes in one direction down a group or across a period; a pattern, not a rule.

workedExample.prompt: Rubidium sits below potassium in Group 1. Using the trends, predict its appearance, density and melting point.
steps: Rubidium lies below potassium, so every Group 1 trend extends one step further.
Softness increases down the group, so rubidium remains a soft grey solid and looks shiny when freshly cut.
Density rises down the group, so rubidium is more dense than potassium, whose density is 0.86 g cm-3.
Melting points fall down the group, so rubidium melts below potassium's 63.5 degrees Celsius.
workedExample.finalAnswer: Rubidium: a soft grey solid, shiny when freshly cut, more dense than potassium (above 0.86 g cm-3), with a melting point below 63.5 degrees Celsius.
